title: Apologiae In Sanctum Hieronimum Libri Duo
author: Rufinus Aquileiensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp388.tmp388.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: 10. Sed in eo te, inquit, arguo, quod Origenem interpretatus es, qui restitutionem omnium dicit futuram, in qua non solum omnes peccatores absolven- dos, sed et ipsum diabolum et angelos ejus quaud que dicit relaxandos esse de poenis, ut restitutio c om- nium consequenter possit intelligi. Et animas ante dicit creatas esse quam corpora, easque de caelo de- ductas, et corporibus insertas.
passages.english: 10. "But I charge you," he says, "with this: that you translated Origen, who says there will be a restoration of all things, in which he says not only that all sinners are to be absolved, but that even the devil himself and his angels are at some point to be released from their punishments, so that the restoration of all can consequently be understood. And he says that souls were created before bodies, and that they were brought down from heaven and inserted into bodies."
passages.notes: 'quaud que' read as 'quandoque'; stray letters (c) and hyphenations treated as scanning artefacts.

passages.original: 15. Sed conlungamus etiam caetera. « Cujus di- versitatis, inquam, caussas plenius tibi in Apologe- tico, quem Pamphilus pro libris ipsius Origenis scripsit, edidimus, brevissimo libello superaddito, in quo evidentibus, ut arbitror, probamentis, cor- ruptos esse in quamplurimis ab haereticis et male- volis libros ejus, ostendimus, et praecipue istos quos nunc d exigis, ul interpreter, id est, nspi A’/>χών, quod vel de Principiis, vel de Principatibus dici potest, qui sunt revera (??) et obscurissimi et difficil- limi.
passages.english: 15. But let us join on the rest as well. "The causes of this diversity," I said, "we have set out for you more fully in the Apology which Pamphilus wrote on behalf of the books of Origen himself, adding a very short booklet in which, by evident proofs, as I think, we showed that his books have been corrupted in very many places by heretics and ill-wishers, and especially those which you now demand that I translate, that is, the Peri Archōn, which can be rendered either 'On First Principles' or 'On Principalities', which are in truth both very obscure and very difficult."
passages.notes: The Greek title is garbled in the scan ('nspi A’/>χών'); read as Περὶ Ἀρχῶν. 'conlungamus' read as 'coniungamus'; 'exigis, ul' as 'exigis, ut'.

passages.original: Sed iste c alius, quem haec dicere ais, utrum tibi concors et consonans, an vero contrarius sit et immicus, non denegasti. Cum enim alium istum contrarium tibi aliquem nominas, soles ponere quae- dam dicti ejus, sed statim ea destruere et impugna- re : ut Marcionis, et Valentini, et Arii, et caetero- rum. Cum vero alium quidem nominas, et dicta ejus d cum validissimis assertionibus scribis, testimoniis quoque Scripturarum copiosissimis munis, nonne etiam nos tardissimi, et quos tu talpas dicis, videmus istum [Al.
passages.english: But whether this "other person", whom you say says these things, is in harmony and agreement with you, or is in fact opposed and hostile to you, you have not denied. For when you name some "other person" who is opposed to you, you usually set out certain of his sayings, but at once demolish and attack them, as [with those] of Marcion, Valentinus, Arius and the rest. But when you name an "other person" and write out his sayings with the strongest assertions, and fortify them too with the most abundant testimonies of the Scriptures, do not even we, the slowest of wits, whom you call moles, see that this [man]
passages.notes: "c" and "d" are footnote marks, omitted. "immicus" read as "inimicus" (hostile); "munis" as "munis" from munire (fortify). "[Al." opens a variant reading ("istius") completed in the following context; the sentence continues there.

passages.original: Nisi forte et in vinculis absque vinculis computandus est, qui conver- sationem habet in codis;et de quo dici potest : Vos autem inbcarcere (??) estis, nec in carne, sed in spiritu, si tamen spiritus Dei habitat in vobis (Rom. 8. 9·). » Item de cadent re, ex Commentario Epistolae Pauli ad Philemonem sub eo capitulo, ubi ait : Salutat te Epa- phras concaptivus metis (Phil. 1. 23.) : post aliquanta : « Nisi forte reconditum aliquid et sacratum, ut quidam putant, in verbo captivitatis ostendit [Al. ostenditur], quod capti pariter et vincti, in vallem hanc deducti sunt lacrymarum.
passages.english: Unless perhaps he too, even in chains, must be reckoned as without chains, who has his way of life in the heavens, and of whom it can be said: "But you are not in prison, nor in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you" (Rom. 8:9). Likewise on the same subject, from the Commentary on Paul's Epistle to Philemon, under the section where he says, "Epaphras, my fellow captive, greets you" (Philem. 23): after some intervening matter: "Unless perhaps he shows [Al. it is shown] something hidden and sacred, as some think, in the word 'captivity', namely that, captured and bound together, they were led down into this valley of tears."
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: "codis" read as "caelis" (heavens); "inbcarcere (??)" as "in carcere", evidently with a dropped "non" (the quotation adapts Rom. 8:9, where Paul says "you are not in the flesh"); "cadent re" as "eadem re" (same subject); "metis" as "meus" (my). The edition's reference "Phil. 1. 23" should be Philemon 23.

passages.original: (??) Et si Clemens, aut ille Apostolorum discipulus, aut ille Alexandrina Ecclestae, et ipsius 352 magister Origenis tale aliquid dixerunt : etiamsi Gregorius ille Ponticus, vir Apostolicarum virtutum : etiamsi iste alius Nazianzenus, et Didyimus videns Propheta, ambo magistri mei quibus sapientius in fide Christi nihil habuit mundus. Omnes isti ut Origenes erra- verunt; sed accipiant erroris sui veniam, quia et e(??)d aliquando erravi, et nunc poenitentiam gero, sed ve- niam accipere debeo. Origenes vero cum eadem quae ego dixerit, etiamsi poenitentiam egit [Al.
passages.english: And if Clement, either that disciple of the Apostles, or that [Clement] of the Alexandrian Church and teacher of Origen himself, said anything of the sort; even if that Gregory of Pontus, a man of apostolic virtues; even if that other, the Nazianzen, and Didymus the seeing prophet, both my teachers, than whom the world has had nothing wiser in the faith of Christ — all of these erred as Origen did; but let them receive pardon for their error, since I too once erred, and now I am doing penance, and ought to receive pardon. But Origen, though he said the same things as I, even if he did penance [another reading: should have done penance],
passages.notes: The passage is Rufinus's ironic paraphrase of Jerome's position. Sentence ends incomplete; continued in following context. 'e(??)d' read as 'ego'. The first Clement may be Clement of Rome, the second Clement of Alexandria; the Latin is compressed.

passages.original: Superiore quidem libello dogmaticas illius ob- jectiones quas aliis impingit immerito, in se, b ipso teste retorsimus : nunc vero jam explicitis et post tergum rejectis bis, quae fidei vicinae sunt c cans- sationibus, confidentius ei de caeteris criminationi- bus respondebimus. Est enim etiam illud accusatio- nis ejus gravissimum caput, quod similiter, ut cae- tera mendacia, veritatis falce resecandum est. Ait enim confoederatos esse quosdam Origeni ad per- jurium, et istud mysticae ejus traditionis areanum absconditum esse in sexto Stromatum libro : ned ab ullo alio d in tot saeculis 355 nisi a se solo deprehensum. Verum ne risum ei moveam, si juris- jurandi sacramento alienum me esse confirmem, a confoederatione perjurii planiore via ad manifes- tationem veritatis incedam, ex eo [Al.
passages.english: In the former book we turned back upon himself, with himself as witness, the doctrinal objections which he undeservedly hurls at others; but now, having dealt with and cast behind us these pretexts, which border on the faith, we shall answer him with more confidence about his other charges. For there is also this most serious head of his accusation, which, like his other lies, must be cut away with the sickle of truth. For he says that certain people are sworn into a league with Origen for perjury, and that this secret of his mystical tradition is hidden in the sixth book of the Stromateis, and has been detected by no one else in so many centuries except by himself alone. But so as not to give him occasion for laughter if I were to affirm by the sacrament of an oath that I am a stranger to the league of perjury, I shall proceed by a plainer road to the disclosure of the truth, from this [another reading: and to him]:
passages.notes: 'canssationibus' read as 'causationibus' (pretexts); 'areanum' as 'arcanum'; 'ned' as 'nec'. The final clause runs into the following context.

passages.original: Restdente in tribunalibus judice f Domino Jesu Christo, assistentibus Angelis, et Intercedentibus pro se, inter verbera et cruciatus jurat se saeculares libros nec habiturum unquam, nec lecturum. Relegantur nunc, quaeso, quae scribit, si una ejus Operis pagina est, qux non eum iterum Ciceranianum pronuntiet, ubi non dicat : sed Tullius noster, sed Flaccus noster, sed [Al. et] Maro. Jam vero Chrysippum et Aristidem, Empedoclem, et caetera Graecorum auctorum nomina, ut doctus vi- deatur, et plurimae lectionis, tanquam fumos 360 et nebulas lectoribus spargit.
passages.english: With the Lord Jesus Christ sitting as judge on the tribunal, the angels standing by and interceding for him, amid blows and tortures he swears that he will never possess, nor read, secular books. Now let what he writes be read over again, I ask, [to see] whether there is a single page of his work which does not again declare him a Ciceronian, where he does not say, 'But our Tully,' 'But our Flaccus,' 'But [another reading: and] Maro.' And indeed he scatters Chrysippus and Aristides, Empedocles, and the other names of Greek authors before his readers like smoke and mist, so that he may seem learned and of very wide reading.
passages.notes: Refers to Jerome's dream in Ep. 22. 'Aristidem' may be an error for Aristotle or Aristides; left as written.

passages.original: Jam vero in illo libello, quem de Optimo ge- nere interpretandi intitulavit, ubi praeter tituli an- notationem nihil optimum, sed totum pessimum est (ibi enim asseverat haereticos illos, quibus nunc b communicat, et incurrit illam sententiam Apostoli nostri, non sui, ille enim suum aut Flaccum dicit, aut Tullium, qui ait : Qui autem [Al. enim] discer- nit, si manducat, damnatus est [Rom. 14. 23.]), in illo ergo libello, c quod nullo genere verbum de verbo interpretari ratio sinat (quod modo ei iterum rationabile visum est), capita integra dictata ex co- dice Ciceronis inseruit.
passages.english: Then again, in that booklet which he entitled On the Best Kind of Translating, where apart from the wording of the title nothing is best but everything is worst (for there he declares heretics those with whom he now communicates, and he incurs that sentence of our Apostle — not his, for he calls Flaccus or Tully his own — who says: 'But he who discriminates, if he eats, is condemned' [Rom. 14:23]), in that booklet, then, [arguing] that reason permits in no way the translating of word for word (which has just now again seemed reasonable to him), he inserted whole chapters dictated from a copy of Cicero.

passages.original: Nam Por- phyrius tuus, 368 dic quaeso, quid te docuit, qui adversum Christianos, et adversum religionem nos- tram blasphemiae volumina conscripsit? Quid te isti in quibus tantum te jactas, unus ab idolis dae- monum, et alius d de Synagoga, ut dicis, Satanae magistri docuerunt boni? Nihil video nisi hoc quod et ipsi noverant. Nam Porphyrius te docuit de Christianis male loqui, concidere virgines, conti- nentes, Diaconos, Presbyteros, et omnem prorsus Christianorum gradum et ordinem libellis editis infamare. Ille vero de Synagoga Barrabas tuus pro Christo electus, docuit te resurrectionem carnis, non in virtute, sed in fragilitate sperare : literae occidentis amicum fieri, et inimicum spiritus vivi- ficantis.
passages.english: For your Porphyry — tell me, please — what did he teach you, who wrote volumes of blasphemy against Christians and against our religion? What good did these teachers of yours, in whom you boast so much, teach you — the one from the idols of demons, and the other from the synagogue, as you say, of Satan? I see nothing except what they themselves knew. For Porphyry taught you to speak ill of Christians, to cut down virgins, the continent, deacons, presbyters, and to defame in published booklets absolutely every rank and order of Christians. But that Barabbas of yours from the synagogue, chosen in place of Christ, taught you to hope for the resurrection of the flesh not in power but in weakness; to become a friend of the letter that kills, and an enemy of the Spirit that gives life.
passages.notes: 'Barrabas' is Rufinus's punning name for Jerome's Jewish teacher Bar-Anina.

passages.original: Et quamvis ei sufficere ad silentium agendum debeat, quod ea in alienis li- teris culpat, quae proferuntur ex suis; tamen et in hoc quam verum dixerit, videamus. Ex Praefatione interpretationum in Ezechiele, quatuordecim Homi- liis, sive Oratiunculis Origenis, scribens cuidam Vin- centio : « Magnum est, inquit, f mi amice, quod postu- las, ut Origenem faciam Latinum, et hominem juxta Didymi videntis sententiam, alterum post Apostolos Ecclestarum magistrum etiam Romanis auribus do- nem.
passages.english: And although it ought to be enough to reduce him to silence that he blames in others' writings what is brought forward from his own, still let us see how truly he has spoken in this as well. From the preface to the translations on Ezekiel, the fourteen homilies or little discourses of Origen, writing to a certain Vincentius: "It is a great thing, my friend," he says, "that you ask, that I make Origen Latin, and present also to Roman ears the man who, according to the judgement of Didymus the seeing, is the second teacher of the churches after the Apostles.

passages.original: 15. Item ex Praefatione Commentarii in Michaeam scripta ad Paulam et Eustochium, post aliquanta : « Nam quod dicunt Origenis me volumina compilare, et contaminare non decere scripta Veterum, quod illi maledictum vehemens existimant, eam laudem ego duco maximam, cum illos imitari volo, qui cun- ctis prudentibus et nobis [Al.
passages.english: 15. Likewise from the preface of the Commentary on Micah, written to Paula and Eustochium, after a little: "For as to their saying that I plunder the volumes of Origen, and that it is not fitting to contaminate the writings of the ancients — which they consider a strong reproach — I count it the highest praise, since I wish to imitate those who please all prudent men and us [another reading:
passages.notes: Text breaks off mid-variant; continued in following context ('you').

passages.original: Item de Epistola ad Marcellam : « Ambrosius, quo chartas, sumtus, notarios ministrante, tam in- numerabiles libros vere Adamantius noster et Chal- centerus explicuit, in quadam Epistola, quam ad eundem de Athenis scripserat, refert nunquam se cibos, f Origene praesente, sine lectione sumsisse, 371 nunquam inisse somnum, nisi unus e fratribus sacris Literis personaret. Hoc diebus egisse vel no- ctibus, ut et lectio orationem susciperet, et oratio lectionem.
passages.english: Likewise from the Letter to Marcella: "Ambrose, who supplied the papers, the expenses and the stenographers by which our truly Adamantius and Chalcenterus produced so innumerable books, relates in a certain letter which he had written to him from Athens that he never took food in Origen's presence without reading, and never went to sleep unless one of the brothers was sounding forth the sacred Scriptures. This he did by day and night, so that reading followed prayer, and prayer reading.
passages.notes: *Adamantius* ('man of steel') and *Chalcenterus* ('bronze-guts') are epithets for Origen. 'ad eundem de Athenis' is odd; the letter's recipient is unclear.

passages.original: 19. Sed fortasse dices mihi; Quid superfluis reples paginas? Nunquid et ille dicit criminis i esse nomi- nari Origenem, aut ingenii ei laudem dari? Si praedi- catur talis ac tantus vir, eo magis, si qua sunt illius, in quibus aul apostolicus vir, aut Ecclestae magister dicitur, ul in superioribus ipse profert : aut si quid tale est quod fidem ejus, non ingenium solum com- mendare videatur. Hoc quidem faciam, tamen idcirco k haec protuli, ubi cum talem ac tantum virum dicit, quia in ea Praefatiuncula, ubi eum dicit Apostolum, vel Prophetam defendi, vel usque ad coelum ferri : hunc puto sermonem 372 laudis ejus inscriptum. Et sicubi forte scientiam ejus laudavimus, tales sunt omnes meae in illum laudes, pro quibus hic tantum in te ignis accendit, quas de suis scriptis nec impu- tari sibi dignum ducit.
passages.english: 19. But perhaps you will say to me: "Why do you fill pages with superfluous matter? Does he too say that it is a crime for Origen to be named, or for praise of his talent to be given him?" [It is,] if such and so great a man is proclaimed, all the more so if there are passages of his in which [Origen] is called either an apostolic man or a teacher of the Church, as he himself sets out above; or if there is anything of such a kind that it seems to commend his faith, and not his talent alone. This I will indeed do; yet I have brought these things forward for this reason, where he calls him "such and so great a man": because in that little Preface, where he says that an Apostle or a Prophet is being defended, or is being exalted to the very heavens, I think this language of praise of him is written. And if anywhere perhaps we have praised his learning, all my praises of him are such as these, for which so great a fire is kindled against you here, [praises] which he does not think it fit to have charged against himself from his own writings.
passages.notes: The passage is syntactically difficult and probably corrupt; "aul" read as "aut", "ul" as "ut", "ubi cum" is obscure, perhaps for "ubi eum". The speaker shifts between third person and "you" (Jerome). "i" and "k" are taken as footnote marks. The rendering "[It is,] if" for "Si praedicatur" is conjectural.

passages.original: Sed profer, inquit, ubi eum ita laudaverim, ut fidem ejus excusarem. Non aeque quidem; sed quo- cunque duxeris sequar. Libellum quemdam scribens, comprehendere quasi indiculo quodam voluit, quanta apud Latinos Varro scripserit, et quanta apud nostros Origenes in Graecis, in qua ita ait, « Marcum Teren- tium Varronem miratur antiquitas, quod apud Lati- nos tam innumerabiles libros scripserit. Graeci Chal- centerum miris efferunt laudibus, quod tantos libros composuerit, quantos quivis nostrum alienos sua manu describere non possit.
passages.english: "But show me," he says, "where I praised him in such a way as to excuse his faith." Not in the same way, indeed; but wherever you lead I will follow. Writing a certain little book, he wanted to set out, as if in a kind of catalogue, how much Varro wrote among the Latins and how much Origenes, among our [writers], wrote in Greek, in which he speaks thus: "Antiquity admires Marcus Terentius Varro because among the Latins he wrote such innumerable books. The Greeks extol Chalcenterus with marvellous praises, because he composed as many books as any one of us could not copy out, [even] others' [books], in his own hand."
passages.notes: "Non aeque quidem" is terse; the sense may be "Not equally [with Origen's own praise]" or a concession that the praise was not of the same kind. Chalcenterus ("Brazen-guts") is the nickname of the Greek scholar Didymus.

passages.original: 23. Ecce quae de Origene et de Ambrosio g sentiat. Quod si negare voluerit hoc quod omnes sciunt, quia de sancio Ambrosio dixerit, primo ex eo convin- cetur, quod apud Latinos ipsius tantum, et non alte- rius in Lucam Commentarius fertur. Deinde scit me habere Epistolam suam, in qua hoc h ipsum de aliis excusans, in illum convertit suspicionem.
passages.english: 23. See what he thinks of Origen and of Ambrose. But if he should wish to deny what everyone knows, that he said it of Saint Ambrose, he will be refuted first by the fact that among the Latins a Commentary on Luke by him alone, and by no one else, is in circulation. Second, he knows that I have a letter of his in which, excusing this very thing as referring to others, he turns the suspicion onto [Ambrose].
passages.notes: "g" and "h" taken as footnote marks. The last clause is ambiguous: "in illum" may refer to Ambrose or to someone else.

passages.original: Etiam ipse [Forte ibi] vidisti, quam similes per om- nia esse Origenis sensibus inventi sunt, imo [Al uno] et plus aliquid, quam hoc quod damnari expostulas, continere. Et nisi ipse de his jam tibi exclusisses poenitentiae facultatem, dicens, « Revolvite Commen- tarios meos in Epistolam ad Ephestos, et inde agno- scetis, quomodo Origenis dogmatibus adversatus sum. » 383 Fortassis velles iterum et de his poeni- tere, et in istis condemnare temetipsum, sicut et in caeteris. Tamen quantum in me est, concedo ego tibi et pro his poenitere : sed et pro omnibus non solum, quae locutus es, sed et quae locuturus es, si agas poenitentiam, bene facis.
passages.english: You yourself also saw how they were found to be similar in every respect to the views of Origen, indeed to contain something even more than what you demand be condemned. And had you not yourself already shut off for yourself the opportunity of repenting of these, by saying, "Go through my Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and from them you will recognize how I have opposed the doctrines of Origen," perhaps you would wish to repent of these too, and to condemn yourself in them as in the rest. Yet, as far as it lies with me, I grant you leave to repent of these as well; indeed, if you do penance not only for everything you have said, but also for what you are going to say, you do well.
passages.notes: The edition records the variants "Forte ibi" (perhaps "there") and "uno" (for "imo"). "383" is a page number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Quae utrum sua sint, ut dicis, an ab aliis inserta, ut nos putamus, Deus viderit. A nobis interim ubi ad fidei fastigium et veritatem ventum fuerit, respuuntur. Tu tamen dic, quid exposcis a nobis : haereticum vis ut dicamus Origenem? Hoc fecisse nos, h culpas. Sed catholicam? Pro hoc nos accusas. Destgna mani- festius, quid velis, si tamen potes aliquid horum medium invenire, quod velis. Isti sunt omnes sales tui de Alexandri, et Porphyrii, et ipsius Aristotelis acumine congregati.
passages.english: Whether these [passages] are his, as you say, or inserted by others, as we think, God will see. Meanwhile, whenever we come to the summit and truth of the faith, they are rejected by us. But you tell us what you demand of us: do you want us to call Origen a heretic? You blame us for having done so. Catholic, then? For this you accuse us. Indicate more clearly what you want, if indeed you can find some middle course between these that you want. These are all your witticisms, gathered from the subtlety of Alexander, and Porphyry, and Aristotle himself.
passages.notes: "h" taken as a footnote mark. Alexander is presumably Alexander of Aphrodisias.

passages.original: Sed ponamus, quod non sit Martyris libellus iste, sed cujuscunque unius de Ecclesta, nunquid suis verbis usus est, quisquis ille est Scriptor, ut meritis d cedendum vi- deatur auctoris? De ipsis Origenis voluminibus ponit exempla, et quid de singulis sentiat, non sui defen- soris verbis, sed ejus ipsius, qui accusabatur, osten- dit. Et sicut adversum te modo, multo meis verbis vehemenliora sunt tua scripta : ita illum non excu- santis auctoritas, sed sua dicta defendunt.
passages.english: But let us suppose that this little book is not the Martyr's, but that of any one member of the Church at all. Did that writer, whoever he is, use his own words, so that it should seem one must yield to the merits of the author? He sets out examples from the very volumes of Origen, and he shows what [Origen] thought on each point, not in the words of his defender, but in those of the man himself who was being accused. And just as now, against you, your own writings are far more forceful than my words, so too it is not the authority of the one excusing him that defends him, but his own sayings.
passages.notes: The "Martyr" is presumably Pamphilus, author of the Apology for Origen. "d" taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: Aut etiam si habet, non statim discutiendus est ille, qui pauca interpretatus est, quare non plura, aut cur non illa, sed illa. Li- bertas est enim in hujuscemodi opere, et est vel in arbitrio scribentis, vel in destderio deposcentis; et tamen de sancio Hilario dicit, et de sancto Victori- no : quorum alterum interpretis titulo nihil omnino arbitror transtulisse de Graeco : alterum ipse dicit. Heliodori cujusdam Presbyteri usum scientia, ut quae ille sibi hauriret ex fonte Graecorum, ipse Latino ea sermone digereret, pro eo quod a aut nihil aut pa- rum Graece nosset.
passages.english: Or even if he does have [such knowledge], one who has translated little is not at once to be called to account for why [he did] not [translate] more, or why not these [works] but those. For there is freedom in work of this kind, and it lies either in the choice of the writer or in the wish of the one who asks for it. And yet he speaks of Saint Hilary and of Saint Victorinus: of whom the one, I think, translated nothing at all from the Greek under the title of translator; of the other he himself says that he made use of the learning of a certain presbyter Heliodorus, so that what that man drew for him from the spring of the Greeks, he himself set out in the Latin tongue, because he knew either no Greek or little.
passages.notes: "a" before "aut" taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: 36. Sed et Origenes, inquit, asteriscos fecit, ex translatione Theodotionis assumens, ut componeret volumina, quae appellantur Hexapta. Et quid Orige- nem istum, quando tibi f placet condemnandum, quando placet imitandum producis.
passages.english: 36. "But Origen too," he says, "made asterisks, taking [material] from the translation of Theodotion, in order to compose the volumes which are called the Hexapla." And why do you bring forward this Origen, when it pleases you, as one to be condemned, and when it pleases you, as one to be imitated?
passages.notes: "Hexapta" read as "Hexapla"; "f" taken as a footnote mark.
